subtopic: NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS-PUBLICATION OP NAMES OF OWNERS, STOCKHOLDERS, ETC.

speechtext:
Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview) moved the second reading of Bill No. 20, to amend the Post Office Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is commonly known as the newspaper bill. This legislation was introduced into the house in 1909 by one of the most prominent members of the Liberal party, a great, patriotic citizen, the late Hon. Mr. Lemieux, who so ably presided over this house for many years. It is the law in England, the United States and Australia.
This bill has been before the house since 1925. It came up in that year and in 1926; in 1927 it passed the House of Commons unanimously. It was brought up in 1928, 1929, 1930 and 1935, and now it is being brought forward once more in 1938. That makes eight times it has been introduced in this house. In the other place this bill has been rejected, but no grounds have been given for that rejection. This bill is valid, as was decided by the Supreme Court of Canada the other day in connection with the Alberta legislation.

Post Office Act-Newspapers
Mr. Justice Cannon on behalf of the court delivered a strong judgment, in which he said that the Alberta press bill was an invasion of the field of criminal law and a retrograde step to an early day when any criticism of the government was a crime. Mr. Justice Cannon said:
The federal parliament is the sole authority to curtail, if deemed expedient and in the public interest, the freedom of the press and the equal rights in that respect of all citizens throughout the dominion.
These subjects were matters of criminal law before confederation, have been recognized by parliament as criminal matters and have been expressly dealt with by the criminal code.
No province has the right to reduce in that province the political rights of its citizens as compared with those enjoyed by the citizens of other provinces of Canada.
The subject matter of this bill has been before the house for many years. As is well known, the object of the bill is to identify the ownership of the newspapers. For many years past the newspapers have been coming to parliament and securing privileges. Prior to 1882 newspapers were carried free by the Post Office Department. This bill requires what is the law in England, the United States and Australia, namely, a sworn statement of the names of the owners, editors, publishers and stockholders of every newspaper, magazine, periodical or other publication, which shall be filed with the Postmaster General semiannually. It is not proposed that the Postmaster General shall say what shall appear in the newspapers. That is for the editors or the directors to say; but the Postmaster General is in charge of the administration of the postal laws of this country, and he possesses the same privileges, rights and functions as are possessed by the Postmaster General of England. He may deny the use of the mails to anyone he wishes, without giving any reasons at all. There is in my bill an exception covering religious, fraternal, temperance, scientific and other similar publications, and it is not necessary to file the names of the small stockholders, those owning less than one per cent of the total amount of the stocks, bonds, mortgages or other securities. Any publication which fails to comply with these provisions is to be denied the privileges of the mails. Paid advertising shall be plainly marked, and statements required under the act shall be made in duplicate and delivered to the Postmaster General, who shall make regulations for carrying out the provisions of the act.
I introduce this bill solely in the public interest and in the interests of the press of a liberty-loving country. The bill speaks' for itself. It passed the House of Commons
unanimously on a previous occasion, but was turned down in another place. There are some thirty-six newspapers in Canada which are in favour of the bill; I need not cite them. This legislation is also supported by the assistant postmaster general of the United States, whose letter will be found in Hansard for 1935. He states:
The purpose and intent of the law is to discover the real owners of publications entered as second-class matter and to let the public know who controls the editorial policies of the publication. It has been helpful in many instances where it was necessary to ascertain the actual ownership of publications and has also been beneficial in the case of daily publications which are required to show the average daily paid circulation in correcting the practices of some publishers in representing to advertisers a greater circulation for their publication than actually obtained. The law on the whole has been beneficial in its effect.
The law embodied in paragraph 2 of the above mentioned section, requiring editorial or other reading matter for the publication of which money or other valuable consideration is paid, accepted, or promised to be marked with the word "advertisement," enables readers to determine what is advertising and what is reading matter, and since the advertising portion of publications entered as second-class matter, with certain exceptions, is subject to postage at graduated zone rates, according to distance, the rates ranging from one and one-half cents a pound for the first and second zones to seven cents a pound for the eighth zone, while the reading portion is subject to postage at the flat rate of one and one-half cents a pound, regardless of zone, it also facilitates the collection of the proper postage.
So ithere is a bonus, a subvention, a subsidy given the press through the Post Office Department.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on the principle of the bill, because that is all I can deal with on second reading. I cannot go over the various clauses until the bill reaches committee, but I would submit that it is undoubtedly within the jurisdiction of this parliament. I would go further and say that chain newspapers in this country are sounding the death-knell of democracy and of the party system in Canada. If this goes on until 1940 those newspapers will bring about the end of the party system of government. It is not in the interests of the people that we should have these chain newspapers sending out chain letters from Ottawa, one to a Liberal newspaper and another, containing the same subject matter, to a Conservative newspaper, so that the people do no*t know who is behind it. A few years ago the Canadian Press-I think it is still in existence though I do not know where it is this year- was given a subsidy of $50,000 a year. That was questioned in the house in 1919, when
Post Office Act-Newspapers

Sir Thomas White defended the vote. I believe the two major parties, as well as the other parties to my left, are entitled to have their views presented fairly in the newspapers of Canada. In Ontario the two great parties had that right from the time of confederation, but recently it was taken away. In some newspapers only one side is presented. In my opinion the Canadian Press is just a "me, too" organization. It supports the government of the day, whatever the government of the day happens to ibe.
Public opinion is not going to be always silenced in the province of Ontario by chain newspapers and so on; the political parties are entitled to place their views and policies before the people. That is wthat newspapers are for. A newspaper is, or should be, more than a mere business, though of course there is the business side to it and the most important of all to them. I sympathize with the newspapers in the increased cost of production, and I pay tribute to what the newspapers have done during war times and other periods of unrest. As reported at page 2473 of Hansard of 1935, I paid a great tribute to the press of this country. I said:
The contribution which Canadian newspapers made to the community, the country, education, social benefit, the satisfactory outcome of the war and during the depression; what it did to promote the cause of the poor and needy and of charity and philanthropy and to further every worthy movement on behalf of the soldiers and of the nation at large was invaluable and finds its place on the proudest pages of Canada's history. It was the press that helped very largely to restore Canada to her normal position. Nor can one say too much for the honour and integrity of the press of Canada. The tendency of our Canadian newspapers is decidedly forward, and not backward, and notwithstanding the high cost of material and labour and the depression and the social situation their prospects are bright. I have no doubt that the genius of our newspapers will help to make this country great industrially and socially and in every way, so that Canada will march triumphantly on from strength to strength.
Since that time the position has been to some extent modified. The newspaper is the only medium through which public opinion in the country may be expressed. In that connection possibly I should except the radio. If the free press goes, so go liberty and freedom. Freedom of the press is a social and economic necessity, and was never more necessary than it is to-day. It is essential in connection with popular education.
All the gold in the world will not buy public opinion in Canada. I am sorry that the old Toronto Globe, the organ of George Brown, has since been sold, and has been swallowed

up in a merger with the Mail and Empire, a rather independent paper. We all know about the late Harry Anderson, the Jaffray family and others who stood for high principles. We might not have agreed with them, but I oan tell the house that I introduced the bill because of remarks made to me by the late John R. Robertson, the great battling editor of the Telegram, a patriot and a man who stood for freedom and liberty of the press, and who worked all his life so unselfishly for the common worker, the forgotten man in Canada.
Second, there was H. W. Anderson, the late brilliant editor of the Globe, a Liberal, a man respected in this country. Then, third, and not least, the late Speaker of the house, the Hon. Mr. Lemieux, who deserved credit in connection with this newspaper bill. These three gentlemen persuaded me to take up this work, and I have worked on it for eight years.
In that time there have been newspaper mergers, newspaper chains, and as a result some of the press has been silenced. We have what I would call newspaper cannibalism in Canada. They have been gobbling and swallowing up papers all over Canada. In connection with this newspaper cannibalism may I refer to what the late Speaker of the house, the Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux, said in 1919, as reported at page 1563 of Hansard of April 16 of that year.
Let me give a 'case in point. The Montreal Herald, for over a century, was an old and faithful adherent of the Liberal party. It was the old, recognized organ of the Liberal party amongst the English-speaking minority of my province. It had a large clientele. Suddenly, after the election of 1911, Mr. Brierly who had become the proprietor of that paper, mysteriously sold it first to Mr. MeGibbon, then to Sir Hugh Graham, who afterwards became Lord Atliolstan, both being Tories. But Mr. Brierly was the mask; he was still generally supposed to be the owner. One day Mr. Brierly disappeared. As I said, he first sold the paper to Mr. MeGibbon and Mr. MeGibbon finally sold it to Lord Atholstan, and during all that time the paper retained the appearance of being a Liberal paper, whilst it was kept in existence by Lord Atholstan, only to prevent a rival from coming into the field against the Montreal Star. This was disclosed in a celebrated case in Montreal, and the respectable English-speaking Liberal people of Montreal were shocked to find that such a game had been played at their expense.
In connection with that particular newspaper may I say it was admitted by a gentleman in another section of this building that for many years he was president of that paper, but did not know who owned it. That was admitted right in this building in another place when a similar bill was under discussion.

Post Office Act-Newspapers
Newspaper cannibalism has descended on the county of York and the province of Ontario. The old independent newspapers, the old, country weeklies, have been put out of business by trusts and combines and through restraint of trade. They have driven the independent press, and the views expressed by that press, to the wall. That is the condition so great has been the pressure.
In the city of Toronto we used to have six newspapers. First of all the old Toronto World was driven to the wall. Recent events in Canada call public attention to the question of newspaper ownership and identity. The need for the present measure was never more felt than it is to-day. Where a newspaper owner's treasure is, there will his heart be also. He cannot serve God and mammon. He cannot serve two masters, as the Montreal Herald tried to do. The tied newspaper is a menace to democracy. As I say, if it gives only one side it will destroy the party system by 1940. A newspaper should have no tied financial interests to serve. Some trade journals and fashionable social weeklies may render service to the banks, and so on. But a tied newspaper has neither eyes to see nor ears to hear when it has the financial people behind it. It cannot speak out on an issue of the day. It cannot be loyal to the public, to its readers and at the same time to its financial, invisible backers. I believe it was Macaulay who said that John Wesley had said, in the early days of the new church, "You do not make rich men necessary to you." Those are words of wisdom in connection with a newspaper. A tied newspaper has to look to the invisible man behind the scenes for a statement of policy. The newspapers which are respected are those in the hands of old respected families, the sole concern of which is the operation of newspapers. The chains are the property of those whose outside interests are more important. They are just the loud speakers for the interests they represent.
I am not complaining about the three Toronto newspapers. We know who own them; their identity is well known. I am dealing with the press of Canada as a whole. At page 454 of Hansard for 1928, hon. members will find my observations on the second reading of a bill I introduced at that time in connection with newspaper ownership, and the arguments I adduced in favour of the bill.
The Hamilton Herald has disappeared. The London Advertiser, both morning and evening editions, and the Mail and Empire have all disappeared in a short time. The Herald was founded in 1889, and the Advertiser in 1863. The Mail, which ceased to exist on
November 2, 1936, was founded in 1872, and absorbed by the Empire in 1883.
There has been a disappearance of newspapers in the larger cities of Ontario, Toronto, Hamilton and London, and the discontinuance of those newspapers has thrown many able newspaper men and fine citizens out of work. The name " Mail and Empire " was a name applied to a merger. The Mail was founded in 1872, as a spokesman for Sir John A. Macdonald and a supporter of the national policy. Then it continued operations until it was absorbed in 1937.
As I have said, since confederation the two old political parties had through the press a way of placing their opinions before the people of the provinces. They have had that means since confederation, but now it has been abolished. Money-bags may buy a newspaper; they may bring about mergers and chains; but they should not be allowed to buy public opinion in this country.
We must look at the way in which the liberty of the press has been interfered with in other countries. In the last few days news respecting Germany has been in the forefront. We know that Germany has had propaganda in British newspapers for twenty years. The Morning Post, one of the old patriotic newspapers, has gone. When it ceased publication, the last of the patriotic journals in England vanished. It has been taken over by another paper, the Telegraph. It is interesting to recall some of the speeches delivered at Nuremberg. ' It seems strange to hear these speeches boasting of what Germany had done delivered at a time when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was visiting that country. This is what Doctor Dietrich said:
Liberation of the press from the freedom of the press is one of the greatest historic feats which nazism and fascism have ever accomplished. We have wiped out this freedom of the press-and it is a most glorious achievement.
Is it not a topsy-turvy world when the great rulers boast of having enforced slavery upon their people? If the British Empire is dissolved, the whole world will be in darkness and our lives and liberty will be no more. The decay and decline of the freedom of the press are taking place the world over. There is, in my opinion, no longer any freedom of the press, nor is there any freedom of the pulpit, the legislatures or the universities We can say nothing right here in this house about foreign affairs; no newspaper will mention foreign afairs; but on Sunday I heard over the radio representatives of United States papers relate what this parliament was going to do in regard to foreign affairs. That is what happens when we are afraid to open our mouths in this house in connection with our foreign policy.
Post Office Act-Newspapers

The press of this country are largely to blame for the present state of foreign affairs. With five or six exceptions they failed in their duty. They have all been ready to give lip service to the League of Nations which is now bankrupt, and they have been giving this service for seventeen years. They allowed the finest army and air force and fleet in the world to be scrapped for the benefit of Germany. They encouraged and allowed the armies of France and England to be decreased while Germany was rearming. In my opinion the press, with five or six exceptions, are not doing their duty.
It is interesting to note that the same element is to be found in Great Britain. They are trying to foist a political Anglo-American treaty on the people of that country. This United States agreement will destroy the dominion and the British Empire, and great harm will be done to that Anglo-Saxon federation known as the British Empire. I believe this parliament should do something about the railway situation. I am not going to allow the Canadian National Railways to be thrown to the wolves of private ownership on the urging of newspapers. I believe this parliament should meet this problem as they have done in England and solve it as they did there without anyone losing his job and thus put an end to the $40,000,000 annual deficits.
I do not wish to take up too much time, but I should like, in conclusion, to refer to one or two matters. The Supreme Court of Canada, in upholding the liberty of the press, has rendered a good service to the country. Its decision was that the Alberta press legislation was ultra vires of that legislature. I should like to refer briefly to a report of a special committee of the United States senate which investigated lobbying activities at Washington. Before I quote from this report let me say that a similar condition existed in this country in connection with the evidence given before the mass buying committee. One newspaper was told that if they did not stop referring editorially to the proceedings before that committee certain advertising would be taken out of the paper by big interests. According to the evidence given before this committee of the senate, a similar state of affairs existed in Washington. This investigation was carried on in connection with the president's bill practically to dissolve all holding companies. It was revealed that the duPonts, the Morgans and the Youngs had $12,000,000,000 invested in holding companies. The public utilities power ring attempted to intimidate the New York Times, which was told to stop its criticism of the public utilities or certain advertising would be taken

from the paper. I quote from page 987 of the evidence before the United States senate committee as follows:

speechtext:
Well, I might refresh your recollection. Do you remember a telegram that appeared-do you remember an editorial that appeared there that you thought did not show the right spirit on the part of the New York Times, which brought about a desire to consider cancelling advertising with the New York Times?
Mr. Hopson:	Yes; I remember that I told
our people over the telephone that I thought that the New York Times with their editorial policy on public utilities did more harm than all the advertising we could do, did good, and I saw no advantage in putting any advertising in a paper which accepted the money of business corporations who were trying to protect the property of their investors, and then had editorial writers who had so little knowledge of the business and the problems which we were up against that they destroyed all of the advantage of it by half-baked editorials.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS-PUBLICATION OP NAMES OF OWNERS, STOCKHOLDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The long and short of it is that you told them to go and see about stopping those editorials or cancelling the advertising?
Which they did. Canada has been the happy hunting ground of these United States corporations. They have seized the public domain of this country and have control of the resources of our mines, the sea, the soil and the forests. They are able to intimidate our newspapers and they even came up here and intimidated the members of the mass buying committee. They went to one newspaper in this dominion and told them that they must stop writing editorials with reference to the mass buying committee or advertising would be taken away from them. That is the same state of affairs which this committee in Washington investigated.
I have no desire to be unfair to the newspapers. Probably my remarks would not apply to 95 per cent of the newspapers in this country. I have paid them a tribute before. The natural resources of this country are controlled by United States companies, and many of our industries have been underwritten in New York. The duPonts were referred to in the investigation at Washigton. They came across into Canada, and their influence was so great that the head of one of their companies was put in charge of the employment commission. Canadian Industries Limited has underwritten a number of companies in Canada engaged in production and distribution and agriculture. The head is one of the duPont industry in Canada.
I have about forty different Canadian editorials here which I could read in support of my bill, but I shall not do so to-night. Another investigation was held in Washington in connection with the newsprint paper industry.

Criminal Code-Sweepstakes
That was in response to senate resolution No. 337. I do not say that conditions are altogether parallel here in Canada, but I know that in England the German ambassador, Joachim von Ribbentrop told Lord Halifax, the British Foreign Secretary, that he wanted these attacks in the British press on Germany to stop, and stop now, and then he flew back to Berlin. But he was told right in the House of Commons that Great Britain was a free country. He also protested to the United States last fall against attacks in the New York press, and they told him the same thing, that the United States was a free country; and that the government could not control the press.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, has 'been before the house eight times. I can show that the bill is intra vires. I can cite the opinion of the Minister of Justice in 1935, the Hon. Hugh Guthrie, who, when he was asked by the hon. member for Comox-AIberni (Mr. Neill) whether subsection 2 was intra vires, replied:
I have no objection to expressing my own personal opinion, but I believe it is the rule that it is not proper to ask for legal opinions from the Minister of Justice in regard to these matters. However, I think that the section referred to is within the competence of this parliament if it sees fit to enact it.
When the bill is in committee I shall be glad to answer any questions in regard to the clauses of the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT SWEEPSTAKES ORGANIZED BY PROVINCES FOR BENEFIT OF UNIVERSITIES OR HOSPITALS

speechtext:
Mr. ERNEST BERTRAND (Laurier) moved the second reading of Bill No. 28, to amend the criminal code.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill is to amend section 236 of the criminal code, by repealing paragraph (e) of subsection 6, which is an exception to the holding of lotteries in Canada, and replacing it with the following:
(e) sweepstakes organized by the government of a province of Canada by or under a law of the legislature of such province: Provided there shall not be held more than one sweepstake in any province in each calendar year, and provided also the net proceeds of the sweepstake shall be applied exclusively to or divided amongst recognized and legally constituted universities and/or hospitals of the province as may be determined by the said province.
For the purposes of this paragraph "sweepstake" means a gaming transaction on horse races in the United Kingdom or in Canada and authorized by the legislature of the province of Canada in which the sweepstake is organized.
This question has been debated before in this house. In 1934 the subject was debated when a bill that had passed the senate came before the house. My idea is that the senate is about the same as it was in 1934. Any changes that have taken place in it might or might not be for the better, according to whether we sit here or in another section of this chamber. But the house itself has changed a great deal, and, I would say, for the better.
This is not a political bill. It is a bill on which I understand we can speak our minds, whether we sit on this side of the house or the other.
In the province of Quebec a law was passed in 1934 permitting the operation of lotteries. It is still on the statutes but can not come into operation without an amendment to the criminal code permitting each province to pass a similar law. In the city of Vancouver a plebiscite was held on this question in 1934, with the result that those in favour of lotteries numbered 25,735, as those against, 9,777. I know that in the province of Quebec nobody protested against the law passed during the regime of the late provincial government, and if a plebiscite were held there I am quite sure the result would be almost unanimously in favour of the statute.
The Trades and Labour Congress, on February 14, 1934, also passed a resolution favouring lotteries controlled by government, and that organization represents about 200,000 working men in Canada.
It is a coincidence, Mr Speaker, that the province of Quebec, which has already passed a law for the operation of sweepstakes, and that Vancouver, the metropolis of British Columbia, by plebiscite, should both favour sweepstakes by a large majority, for only a few years ago Quebec and British Columbia
Criminal Code-Sweepstakes

were the first two provinces that dared pass a law for government control of the liquor business. How viciously were they attacked all over Canada for that, and not only in Canada but in the United States! Yet to-day, after a lapse of only a few years, all the other provinces of this dominion have followed the example of Quebec and British Columbia, and the federal government of the United States has also followed suit.
The first reason why I am presenting this bill is to put an end to illegality. Lotteries are being held in Canada whether we like it or not. In Montreal, which is no better and no worse than any other city, we can buy lottery and sweepstakes tickets in every club. They are sold in every club in the city. All the brokers are selling them. Janitors of big buildings have them for sale; not only that, but in many buildings they go from one tenant to another asking him to buy tickets. The elevator boys in downtown buildings have them for sale. If we wanted to stop the sale of these tickets our combined mounted, provincial and municipal police would not be numerous enough; we would have to enlarge the gaols of Quebec to lodge there all those who have been selling and purchasing tickets. Tobacco stores at the corners of the large streets have them for sale, and I know a lot of people who are buying them.

speechtext:
A large number of tickets have been seized during recent years in the principal cities of Canada; but as the law is applied, the police seized the lottery tickets after some of them had been sold for some time, with the result that the lotteries did not take place and the promoters retained the money for the tickets which they had sold. Action of this kind does not repress crime; it is rather an encouragement of it. I sometimes ask myself whether or not the good-for-nothings who are profiting by this system are going to fight the bill affecting this matter, and I am more convinced that, if these good-for-nothings oppose it, the bill is good legislation. Those who would be most opposed to it are those who have been illegally holding lotteries and sweepstakes all over Canada. Some of them are operating in the north country, in the bush, around Lac Tremblant, north of Montreal; they are selling their tickets not only in Canada but all over the United States.
If this law were passed, it would provide large sums to all the provinces for universities and hospitals. I know that every one in this house thinks this bill is intended perhaps to help the university of Montreal. I readily admit that fact, and I ask hon. members who are fortunate enough to come from provinces in which there are universities with rich foundations, universities that do not need to appeal to the poorer sections of the community for assistance, to give favourable consideration to the university of Montreal when they are called upon to cast their votes. After all, universities like Oxford, Harvard, the university of Paris, were all started on lotteries; yet to-day these institutions are not looked down upon because they were born in sin, so to speak, if we do think, as some of our fellow-countrymen do that lotteries are sinful. In the Reader's Digest there appeared, some time ago, an article in which the calculation was made that the sum of three billion dollars was taken out of the United States in three years by foreign lotteries. This does not include the bootleg lotteries operated in the United States. In one instance $17,000,000 worth of tickets were seized, and according to certain figures quoted before an inquiry held in New York I understand that $8,500,000 worth of lottery tickets are sold in New York and New England a month.
We hear a good deal about the moral aspect of lotteries. Well, I respect all opinion so long as it is sincerely expressed; I even respect the opinions of those who are not of
my race or religion. I do not believe, however, anyone can argue that sweepstakes held for the benefit of hospitals or universities are immoral in themselves. After all, if the lotteries are immoral-and I do not admit that they are-they have been permitted for a considerable time in our criminal code, where the object to be won represents less than fifty dollars; and through this section I am seeking to have replaced I do not think that matters will be made any worse.
I have here a book by H. M. Muller on Lotteries. May I read a short passage from it. It is very well written, though I do not think I would go quite as far as this writer does. He says:
A parliament which declines, on grounds of public morality, to countenance national lotteries, while drawing revenue from the drink traffic, and taking toll from public gambling on horses-
He adds dogs, but in Canada we have no dog races.
-is guilty of muddled thinking, or hypocrisy, or both.	*
These are very strong words, and while I would not be prepared to go quite as far as this author does, I quote this passage because I think it is well for every hon. member as well as the public outside to know exactly what other people think about the subject.
I have received a large number of letters, newspaper clippings and resolutions passed by labour unions and municipal councils all in favour of the bill. I have also a statement on gambling and lotteries which has been sent to all the members by the Social Service Council of Canada. As I said a few minutes ago, I respect all opinion, but I find one reason given in this statement which I think should be aired. Let me read it:
Churches, not supported by the state, had to develop a sense of financial responsibility in their membership and created sacrificial giving. To-day, the demands made by the government in various forms of taxation and the multitudinous appeals for secular charities tend to reduce that kind of giving which is created in a sense of religious obligation to meet the needs of our fellow men. It is increasingly difficult for the churches to appeal to the sense of stewai'dship, and if, to all the other difficulties, that created by the establishment of national or provincial lotteries is added-
This is what I wish to emphasize particularly-
[DOT]-the springs of genuine philanthropy will be dried up, and with it the sense of personal responsibility for the well-being of our fellow-citizens.
I do not think the argument is sound that we should not have national lotteries or lotteries held under the authority of the prov-
Criminal Code-Sweepstakes

inces, lotteries for charitable purposes, because the churches are afraid that they will not receive as large sums from their adherents. I do not think the reason is a good one, either from the point of view of the churches themselves or from the point of view of the hospitals and universities. After all, if everyone has a chance to buy a ticket, knowing quite well that his chances are very small indeed, in fact that he has practically no chance of winning, and chooses for the mere pleasure to take that chance, believing that at the same time, even if he loses, he is helping some hospital or university, how will that prevent millionaires from making donations to hospitals and having their own names commemorated in connection with a pavilion or something of that sort? I trust that some better reason can be advanced.

I beg your pardon; I should have said "chart." I quote as follows:
That the best interests of Canada demand that substantial reductions of the burdens of customs taxation be made with a view to the accomplishing of two purposes of the highest importance: First, diminishing the very high cost of living which presses so severely on the masses of the people; second, reducing the cost of the instruments of production in the industries based on the natural resources of the dominion; the vigorous development of which is essential to the progress of our country.
That to these ends, wheat, wheat flour, and all products of wheat, the principal articles of food, farm implements and machinery and repair parts thereof; rough and dressed lumber, gasoline, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils, etc., nets, net twines, and fishermen's equipments; cement and fertilizers, should be free from customs duties, as well as the raw material entering into the same.
Skipping a paragraph which is not material, I read this:
-and the Liberal party hereby pledges itself to implement by legislation the provision of this revision when returned to power.
That platform was adopted by the Liberal party in 1919, and since 1919 that party has been in power eleven years. I think it is noteworthy that the opposition we have heard in this debate to the lowering of the tariff or the elimination entirely of the customs duty on certain farm implements should come from hon. gentlemen who were elected to this house as Liberals. We are told from time to time that the fundamental difference between the Liberal and Conservative parties is that the Liberal party is low tariff while the Conservative party is high tariff. To-day we have witnessed the spectacle of Liberal members rising in their places and urging the retention of present tariff or tariffs.
The report now before the house cost the country a great deal of money. As a member of that committee and as one who is interested in the recommendations contained in this report, I should like to ask the house and the government what we are going to do now that we have the report and its recommendations. To-day various speakers have discussed features of the inquiry brought out during the evidence submitted last summer, and I do not propose to rehash what has been already said to-day. The hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Needham), the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) and others touched upon certain features which I had very much in mind myself.
But what stands out in the report, and in the discussion which led up to that report,

was to me the tremendously great spread between the costs of manufacturing farm machinery and the price the farmer had to pay for it when he bought it. We asked the president of the International Harvester Company what he thought about the costs of distribution, and he admitted that they were too high. We asked him what he proposed to do about the matter, and he said they had been endeavouring to discover more efficient, ways of distributing farm implements. I asked him, if the western farmers established cooperative societies for the distribution of farm implements, would his company, the largest in North America, supply the cooperative societies with implements for distribution? He evaded that question. But a little later in the inquiry the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), at page 492 of the evidence, asked very definitely if the company would supply cooperative societies with agricultural implements, and the answer was a very emphatic no. Consequently I am particularly interested in the recommendation which deals with that very point. We recommend in paragraph 33:
That the committee is of the opinion that the cost of distribution of farm implements is unnecessarily high and constitutes an important factor in the prices to the consumers.
And in paragraph 34:
That the companies themselves should make every effort to reduce these costs or farmers should be encouraged to organize for the cooperative distribution and servicing of farm implements.
To me that is more than a pious hope, and in view of the fact that the farm implement companies have not yet attempted to reduce the admittedly high costs, but on the contrary have in some respects even raised them, I hope that the government in considering the report will make some recommendation to the house for the establishment of cooperative selling agencies at least for the distribution of farm implements in order that they may be distributed at prices more nearly in line with what they ought to be.
The hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) this afternoon defended the companies very ably, I think, but I found myself in disagreement with him except when he deplored the frequent investigations of this industry and the few results that bad accrued to the people of Canada. But after this latest and very thorough inquiry I think the government should act upon such recommendations of the committee as are found to be sound. I believe that the recommendations arrived at, after very careful investigation and very careful consideration of all the evi-

Farm Implements Committee Report
deace, are sound; but so far, as I said before, the companies have done nothing about the matter themselves.
Again I would ask the government and the majority supporting it what they propose to do about this matter. I have not forgotten that some of us two years ago agreed with those who raised this question in the house, with the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Johnston), for example, when he complained of the price of implements; and as will be remembered, when the Canada-United States trade agreement was before the house I moved that farm implements be placed on the free list, as a gesture against what was then being done. But that motion was not pressed because of the inquiry which was then being undertaken. I am hoping now, two years having elapsed, and having had a sufficient opportunity to look into this matter, that the government will take effective steps to see that the farmers not only of the west but of the east are given their agricultural implements at a reasonable price; and not only their implements at a reasonable price, but that the cost of repairs and servicing be looked after for them also, because when we inquired into the cost of repairs we found they were entirely out of line with the cost of new machines.
We are sometimes told that one of the factors accounting for the increased prices is an increase in labour costs; but may I point out that in the last few years the improvements in machinery, reducing the number of men employed and increasing the total output per man in the factory, has in effect not added to the actual cost of labour, and in that respect I find myself not altogether in agreement with one of the conclusions of this report. One difficulty, of course, which we have to face in Canada is that there is a tremendous capital investment in these companies. Like many of our other Canadian industries they have been established and have grown up with the idea that there was more or less an unlimited market, and their capitilization in the aggregate is out of line with the actual requirements of the country in which we live.
Then of course we found, too, that the price of agricultural implements tended to be set by any company which had a virtual monopoly of certain lines of machinery. We found in our investigation that one company, the International Harvester Company, controlled some sixty per cent of the agricultural implement business in Canada; and although that company denied-and I believed the president when he made that denial-that there was any
5X952-87
collusion between the several companies with regard to price fixing, nevertheless I think that practically all the members of the committee were of the opinion that the smaller companies set their prices after they had seen the prices set by the larger implement company. Therefore, in effect, the International Harvester Company did set prices in most lines of machinery for the entire industry.
To those who defend the tariff I would say again that on the prairies, where most of this very high priced machinery has to be used-not is used, but has to be used- the farmer sells his product on the unprotected markets of the world. Consequently, if we are going to give industries and organizations from which he has to buy, protection in this market, obviously we shall have to consider those proposals that have been called in this house "compensating adjustments" of various kinds. If we are going to guarantee to the industrialists a price for their products, then we shall also have to guarantee to the producer minimum prices for the products which he produces.
I confess that in this house there seems not very much likelihood of substantial tariff reductions, because after a period, extending into years, during which the Liberal party have had every opportunity to make those reductions to which they are pledged, and listening to the debates in the house, watching the budgets that have come down, noticing-as I said yesterday-actual increase in the tariff on one necessity of life, furniture, and high duties on other necessities of life, I do not see very much hope from this government in the direction of really lower tariffs.
The hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann) spoke of the competition given C_ local manufacturers from cream separators imported from Sweden. He attributed Swedish ability to export and lay down cream separators in Canada at a much lower price than that at which they could have been manufactured here to the fact that Sweden has a lower standard of living than we have. I do not know where he got the information regarding the average wage of the Swedish worker which he placed at 19J cents an hour, but I do say this, that the International Labour Office at Geneva and observers generally throughout Europe make the statement that the Swedish worker today is the best housed, the best clothed, the best looked after, and in many respects the best-off worker in any European country. Consequently, how can it be said that it is the low standard of life in Sweden which accounts for lower costs of production there

Farm Implements Committee Report
is more than I can understand. Long hours are not in effect there either; the workers are well organized, and the government of Sweden has the most advanced social legislation of any of the European countries.
The hon. member for Renfrew South also said that the reason for the increase in the price of separators laid down in New Zealand in recent years over preceding years was the fact that the Swedish manufacturers had eliminated competition there. I do not know to what extent that is true; but I would draw this to his attention, that in the past few years one factor at least which must have operated was that the New Zealand pound has been greatly depreciated, which means that it would buy less in the markets of the world. Consequently the tendency would be to increase the price as stated in New Zealand pounds; for if four New Zealand pounds of seven or eight years ago have the purchasing power of only five pounds at the present time, it is obvious that a foreign nation axporting to New Zealand will have to increase the price to at least that extent. I would draw that to the attention of the house when we hear of the increased price of cream separators in New Zealand.
As I said before, previous speakers have covered the ground which I intended to cover, and therefore I do not propose to repeat what they have said, because that is wearisome to the house and to anyone discussing the matter. I would simply say again to the government: There is the report on the table; there are the recommendations; the government has an overwhelming majority, a majority which enables it to fulfil every pledge that it has ever made, and one of the definite pledges which the government made through the party which elected it and which formulated the Liberal platform upon which it appealed to the country, was that farm implements would be admitted into this country free of all customs duties. And I say to the government, What are you going to do about this?

The hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Bouchard), speaking this afternoon, made the statement that between 1925 and 1929, when the Liberal government was in power and there were low tariffs, more people were employed in agricultural implement factories than from 1929 to 1932, at a time when the tariff had been increased by the late government. Everyone knows that comparison is most unfair. From 1924 to 1929 were four of the most prosperous years that Canada has ever known. The country had abundant crops; farmers had the purchasing power and were able to buy machinery, and that is why the people were kept at work. In the years between 1929 and 1932 Canada, in common with other countries, was going through one of the worst depressions the world has ever known. There were no crops; farmers had no purchasing power, and the machine companies could not manufacture the machinery because they could not sell it. The tariff played no part in those conditions.
We have been told in the course of this debate that 32 per cent of the agricultural implements sold in Canada are manufactured here, and that 68 per cent of them have been imported into this country. That means that we are sending 68 per cent of our money into a foreign country to pay foreign labourers and to build up foreign institutions instead of having these machines manufactured at home.
There seems to be a common impression among hon. members opposite that high tariffs mean high prices to the consumer. The very opposite is the fact; high tariffs have always meant cheaper goods to the consumer. Take, for instance, farm implements. The former government had a tariff of 25 per cent and along with that an agreement with the companies that if they raised the price to the farmer, that tariff would be reduced. This government came in and cut that tariff down to 7^ per cent, which nullified the agreement made by the former government, and up went the price of farm machinery. Nothing else could be expected, for this reason, that if United States manufacturers are allowed to come in and take 68 per cent of the business of Canada, with the small turnover that our own manufacturers have, the

Farm Implements Committee Report
manufacturers here must necessarily obtain a larger profit or they cannot live. Therefore the lowering of the tariff has cost and will cost our farmers some millions of dollars. History is only repeating itself. We all remember, at any rate I can remember when binder twine, barbed wire and coal oil were put on the free list. What happened? They just doubled in price, and putting these things on the free list has cost the farmers of Canada millions of dollars in the extra money that they have been obliged to pay for barbed wire, coal oil and binder twine.
I have often wondered why our western representatives come into this house and talk the way they do. I have been here for a number of years and I find that year after year they rise in their places and denounce the tariff. They cry for free trade. They would kill the industries of eastern Canada, the industries of Ontario and Quebec; they would put them out of business, and by so doing they would be putting their own customers out of business.
What about the maritimes?

The maritimes are all
right. As I say, these hon. gentlemen would destroy their own customers; and yet some of them will rise in their places here and ask for a few million dollars to buy seed wheat, knowing perfectly well that these very industries in Ontario and Quebec will be called upon to meet the cost, because these two provinces pay between 75 and 80 per cent of the taxes of the entire dominion. Yes; they would bite the hand that feeds them. That is exactly what they have been doing for years. I am willing to help the western farmers, and I think we do help and are only too glad to help them when the grasshoppers eat their crops or when the frost blights them or the drought burns them out. Whenever the western farmers suffer these calamities we come to their assistance. But there is a limit to what we can be expected to do when these very men come here and seek to kill the industries of the country upon which our eastern farmers depend; for let me tell the house that it is the men and women engaged in the industrial' life of the country who make the home, market for the farmer.
Did the increase in the tariff on furniture result in a decrease in price last spring?
We are talking about farm implements.

The importations of
furniture have increased and the price has
also increased. It is higher to-day than it ever was. Let me point out what has happened in connection with farm implements. In 1934 there was 82,850,000 worth of farm implements imported into Canada and in 1936 with the duty lowered the amount was $8,811,000.
Were they not practically all tractors?

No, they were not. In 1937 Canadian farmers sent $16,275,000 for farm implements to fill the pay envelopes of a foreign country and to build up foreign institutions. Then we send men to Washington to get down on their knees and beg these people to allow us to send over some food to them. Our own people should have been manufacturing these implements in Canada and then they would have used our own farm products without hindrance. If we were manufacturing not only farm implements but textiles, also sufficient to supply our own people, there would not be an idle man or woman in the country to-day.
Why were there idle men in 1931?
The Liberal government was too long in power.

The policies which my hon. friend enunciates in this house would beggar the country if they were ever put into operation; they would simply ruin us and make us a nation of beggars. In the Globe and Mail to-day I was struck with something I saw on the front page. The premier of Ontario is reported to have said that in October there were 160,000 people on relief in the province, and that in February, last month, there were 260,000. That will be found on the front page. What is the cause? It is the tariff tinkering of this government, which is putting our people out of work. I know one man who owns several factories. He owned one in a certain town in the Ottawa valley and he decided to tear it down. Why? He said that every time the government changed they were faced with the danger of being put out of business. He said he could employ two hundred people if he could be guaranteed the protection he had between 1930 and 1935, but he would not be tormented by the tinkering with the tariff. He simply decided to tear down his factory, level the ground and turn it into a park.
Our people to-day are being put out of business; people are being forced into the relief lines because our industries are not given the protection they should get. Do you

expect the people of Canada to come down to the standard of living that obtains in these foreign countries from which competition comes? We are proud that Canadian workers can live comfortably and bring up their families and educate them as good Canadians and British subjects, and we do not want to see our standard of living lowered to the level that we see in those countries which are attempting to dump their goods here.
What about the United States?

Who is shouting now? Oh, it is some more of the economists. It appeared to me that the hon. member for Renfrew South placed this matter in a very fair light. He said that if we permitted these companies to go out of business, we would pay a great deal more for our products when they were controlled by a foreign country. As I said a moment ago, we had an example of that in connection with binder twine and barbed wire. What about our binder twine to-day? These United States manufacturers sit down in Chicago and set the price that will be charged in Canada for binder twine. We have allowed our binder twine to get into the hands of a foreign country, and we have been paying through the nose for it. In 1896, when the duty was taken off, we had twenty-five small factories manufacturing binder twine in this country. They were the nucleus of a big business that we might have had, but they were crushed out by the mass production of the United States. Then, when our people were out of business, the United States concerns had us where they wanted us, and to-day they charge what they wish.

Mr. Speaker, at five-thirty this afternoon I was on my feet, and I thought I had a fairly good speech to deliver. Since then, however, I am afraid I have had to scrap most of it, because it has been said by other speakers. Consequently I shall have to satisfy myself by making a few observations. When one follows the hon, member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson) on our side of the house, there is not much left for one to say, because he covers the ground so thoroughly, and I wish to congratulate him upon his splendid address.
I do not agree with the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) when he advocates bringing cream separators into Canada from foreign countries free of duty. He is always good at discussing academic questions, which I do not fully understand; but after all, with all the knowledge he has, he does not seem to appeal to me as a good Canadian, and I do not mind saying so. He is always advocating something that is detrimental to the working people of this country, such as he has suggested to-night.
I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) who made a splendid address, in regard to which his country and his own riding should be tickled to death. It was well delivered, and what he said was absolutely true and to the point. That would have been so regardless of whether it was delivere'd by a Liberal or a Conservative.
It does not matter,' really.

The hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann) did the same thing, and I say he deserves credit for giving us full information as to the difference between wages paid in Scandinavian countries

Farm. Implements Committee Report
and those paid in Canada. I was proud of him to-pight as he stood in his place and delivered an address equal to any I have heard delivered in this house by any Liberal during the seventeen years I have been here. It is not often that the Liberals talk really good common sense, when it comes down to business. They are always opposed to something that will build up the nation. I do not know where they get their ideas.
With my hon. friend the member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) I cannot agree at all. He seems to be out of touch with things. Instead of something sane that a government could adopt, which one would expect from the brilliant chap that he is, we had a stupid recommendation to-night. Everybody knows this country cannot live without protection, and those who do not know it might as well get it into their heads. I see that gradually the light is beginning to dawn. It will seep in further and further until after a while you will get to -the point where you will do something for your country. I hope it will not be too long delayed.
I happened to be on the committee that investigated the prices of farm implements in 1936, but fortunately for the committee, or fortunately for myself, or something, they got rid of me in 1937. A smaller special committee was appointed, and I was laid off. I listened to a great deal of evidence given there that I thought was of very little importance. Some of it was ratheT amusing. I think some hon. members on that committee suggested that the prices of farm implements were entirely too high, and that the people in the west were getting so little for their grain that they could not afford to buy implements at all. They even suggested that these farmers should be allowed to pay just what they thought they could pay, and that the balance should be absorbed by the government or by some organization appointed by the government. That was the kind of stuff one heard on that committee; that was one of the arguments advanced there.
Who argued that?

I do not know. I never keep notes of what hon. members say in the house, so I cannot tell tales. But if you will go back to the records of that committee meeting you will find that two or three hon. members from the west made that suggestion. If there is anything more ridiculous than that, go back to the west and find it. I do not see how you can.
It is unfortunate there is so much time wasted. Hon. members cannot say that I
waste much of the time of the house-perhaps ten minutes a week. Some hon. members start in at three o'clock in the afternoon and do not stop until eleven o'clock at night. Half a dozen of them talk all day, and nobody else gets a word in. Do not forget that. But if I am going to pound a little common sense into some hon. members I must take some time to do it.
We are losing a great deal of time in discussing things of the past. I say we are here to legislate for the future. Let us forget the past. Let us start in to do something for the people here in Canada at the present time. Let us try to get this country back to normal-which we are not doing. We have wasted a lot of time in discussing economic questions and radical resolutions. I think all hon. members and particularly those members to my left, will admit that. A great deal of time has been spent in discussing questions which, in the end, amount to nothing. We have now wasted about two months of the session, and have done nothing. The members of the senate have been going back and forth to their homes. They adjourn for a month; then they come back and adjourn for a week, and still, with the exception of a couple of bills which passed this house, they have had nothing to do. Is that not a waste of time?
Let me tell hon. members that if the people in our ridings could see the way we act in the house, they would ask for a dissolution of the house at once, and advocate the formation of a committee of one hundred, or something of the kind, to run the country. Sometimes I would like to see that myself, because it is a waste of time to have the house sitting with sometimes not more than twenty-five members who are taking any interest in the proceedings. What interest is taken by the members who are supposed to occupy these two lines of benches? You may look anywhere in the house-everywhere. They might as well be home, and not be in Ottawa at all.
Why don't they go?

They have lots of places
to go.

They are working
in their rooms.

Are they? They are playing bridge in some comer! Such intolerable ignorance of business affairs is displayed by some hon. members, something which is astonishing to one who from boyhood has been trained in the business world. It is astonishing to listen to people in the house

Farm Implements Committee Report
who have never sold even a box of matches, or never made a trade in their lives, tell us how to run the country. It is amazing! It is useless discussion.
There can be no doubt that prices of commodities rise and fall. I shall cover this point later on when I discuss the investigation into farm implements. I would repeat that supply and demand will always regulate prices, regardless of any attempts made by governments to regulate people's business and to regulate prices. You cannot get away from the old law of supply and demand, so you might as well make up your minds that you will have to get back to normalcy before the country can make headway.
Many members of the house should still be in kindergarten, so far as any knowledge of business is concerned.
You should be the teacher.

Calamity howling is the principal act in the House of Commons. I came down on the train from Toronto yesterday with a gentleman from Saskatoon, a brilliant chap who said to me that the people in the House of Commons from the western provinces are not representing the viewpoint of people in the west. He said that he disapproves the tactics used by those members who picture the sad scenes of people in distressed circumstances, and all that sort of thing. He said it was not advertising for Canada or for the prairie provinces.
But they are true.

They are not true at all; he says they are not true. There is in the house no more brilliant man than the man with whom I was duscussing the subject yesterday, and he was a Liberal from Saskatoon. You may pick out who he was. He says that Saskatoon is paying its debts and pulling itself out of the hole. You can hear nothing in the House of Commons but calamity howling, all the time. I think that man was a Liberal, although I did not ask him. It makes no difference to me what a man's politics may be. I like to discuss business, whether a man be a Liberal or a Conservative.
He was not brilliant, then.

He was brilliant, too. I would admit that certain Liberals are brilliant; there is no doubt about that.
When the investigation began into the price of farm implements, it was shown that between 1930 and 1936 commodity prices had increased. It was to be expected that to some extent farm implement prices should

increase. The old stocks on hand were gone, and new stock had to be bought. Jf there were increased costs we could not expect the manufacturers to sell at a loss. One hon. member has suggested that the government should absorb the difference between what the farmer could pay and what the manufacturer should get. Did you ever hear such talk as that in your life?
We have heard it from Conservatives for a long time. Protection means the same thing.

speakeroldname: Mr. L. P. A. ROBICHAUD (Kent, NS.):

speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman aware that subsequently to that deputation very important changes were made in the budget and concessions granted to these manufacturers ?

Concessions were made by reducing the tariff on their raw materials; I have no objection to that. Why were they so successful in the two years following the reduction? It is easy to see why. It was for the simple reason that prices went down and people bought automobiles more freely, and although the manufacturers had to accept a smaller profit on each automobile, their aggregate profits at the end of the year showed a large increase. After all, what is the secret of success in any line of merchandising? Is it to sell one article a day and make fifty cents profit on the sale, or is it to sell ten articles a day and make ten cents profit on each article? The more goods you sell the more profit you make and the more service you can give.
Here may I quote, with approval, the statement made by the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman): "There has never in Canadian history been a tariff reduction which did not benefit Canadian manufacturers, but they fear it." Ah! Fear! Fear! That is it. Fear, which at one time was no doubt the natural and normal reaction of man in his primitive state and was intended as a necessary shield for his self-preservation, has to-day become a heavy and burdensome armour, impeding him in his upward march towards a higher civilization. That fear which in those days was a physical, bodily fear, and quite normal, has to-day become simply an atavic, mental and moral fear-the curse of humanity, and man's greatest enemy.
If I were-I was going to say if I were king, but I will put it in a more modem way -if I were the dictator of Canada, do you

Farm Implements Committee Report
know what I would do, Mr. Speaker? I would issue a decree to take effect to-morrow morning, establishing absolute free trade in this country.
Oh.

It may surprise some hon. members, since I am not a resident of the west or a farmer, when I proclaim myself a one-hundred per cent unadulterated free trader. But someone will say: "If you do that, you will flood the country with foreign goods." I say then, and in the spirit in which the apostle of the gentiles uttered his famous exclamation "O Felix Culpa," Happy flood, blessed flood! The flood would continue only so long as we were able to pay for the goods, and so long as we were able to pay for them we would be prosperous indeed.
If, however, my decree is going to disrupt confederation, and if we are everlastingly to continue bonusing and subsidizing industry at the expense and to the detriment of the primary producers and of the consumers of Canada generally, then I say, Mr. Speaker, let us have an honest-to-goodness, open and above board system of bonusing. Let us, as I said, abolish tariffs, and then at the end of a year, or semi-annually, let us bonus the legitimate natural industries of the country which prove themselves unable to carry on under a system of free trade. We have been bonusing wheat in the past, and bonusing to some slight extent the fishermen of the maritime provinces; but we know exactly to a cent what these bonuses have cost us, and I am sorry to say that on many occasions we have begrudged granting these bonuses to the poor farmer and the poor fisherman. But we do not know, and we cannot tell, how many millions or hundreds of millions of dollars we have been giving in bonuses to industry in Canada by means of the tariff. I think we should take the means to know, and the only way to know is to bonus them directly. Let us have free trade; let them compete with the goods coming from other nations, and let us bonus those industries that cannot carry on under free trade. But many of them are artificial industries which should never have been established in this country. They are economically unsound, and under free trade they would be given a chance to disappear as, to my mind, they should disappear.
As I have said before in the house-and I am convinced of it-the economic situation of this world will never be righted before we have free trade throughout the world and before the nations of the world make up their minds to manufacture the commodities for which they have the raw materials. Does it
stand to reason that nations should spend millions and billions of dollars in removing natural obstacles from the channels of trade, in building railroads, and digging canals, and then the moment after erect artificial obstacles to trade by way of tariff walls? No, Mr. Speaker, it does not stand to reason. The thing is unnatural, and for that reason it will have to disappear from the face of the earth. And so it is with great pleasure that I support the motion of the hon. member for Lake, Centre.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to refer to some of the remarks made by hon. members who have spoken to-night.
The hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson) claimed that 68 per cent of our machinery was imported, and he deplored that fact. We might deplore anything of that nature under certain conditions; but in a country like Canada we must import if we are going to export, and it stands to reason that if we are importing so many of these implements or any other products and are paying out so many millions of dollars for them, that only enables us to sell millions of dollars worth of our own products abroad. I know the hon. member for Lanark pretty well, and respect him very much. I remember he came into my constituency in 1925 and was instrumental in defeating me at that time. I have no hard feelings against him for that. But I wish the Conservative party would send him out at the next election and let him make a speech like he made to-night.
I will do it.
You are invited, and I hope they will do that.
Does the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) not want to come back here again?

I am sorry that the hon. member found it necessary to use the words, "The western people would bite the hand that feeds them." He followed that up, it seemed to me, in an apologetic way by saying that we should cease flying at each other's throats
Certainly.
How do the sales compare in those years?

The sales had a great deal to do with their profit, because, as I said at the beginning, we were partners in a great business, and when one partner was a little bit down, not as flush as usual, the other suffered also.

But how were the sales
in those various years? Was production up or down?

The sales were not so good after 1930. Possibly that was because the tariff had been increased and there may have been other causes; personally I believe the depression had a great deal to do with the matter, because there was not the purchasing power.

A great deal would
depend on the number of units built in the year.

That is so. It would be interesting to the house to have a comparison of the farmers' position during those years. I have here a table prepared at my request by the bureau of statistics. I have selected eight farm implements which the
ordinary farmer must have if he is to make any pretence of farming, and in the same table I give the prices of steers. The table shows what the farmer had to pay in hundredweight of steers for these various implements. These are the prices of steers at Winnipeg. If I may put the whole statement on Hansard I shall net go into the figures extensively tonight, but shall cite simply one or two. In 1913 we received 6-63 cents per 100 pounds for "good" steers, live weight, at the Winnipeg stock yards. And remember, over fifty per cent of the steers are not graded "good." However, to give the manufacturers the benefit of the doubt I am quoting these figures. In that year, 1913, we could buy a walking plough for 300 pounds of steers. In 1920, although the price of walking ploughs had gone up, we could still buy a walking plough for 300 pounds of steers. In 1926 the price of steers had gone down and we could buy a walking plough for 500 pounds of steers. In 1932, with a still lower price for steers, we had to give 700 pounds in exchange for a walking plough. In 1913 we gave 2,600 pounds of steers for a binder; in 1920, 2,300 pounds; in 1926, 4,800 pounds; in 1932, 6,100 pounds; and in 1936, 6,100 pounds.
